item.title: Sophos AI Defense is now generally available
item.description:
When we introduced Sophos AI Defense in July, we focused on a challenge facing organizations everywhere: 

AI adoption is accelerating, often faster than security and IT teams can see or control it. New AI tools, embedded capabilities, and shadow AI are creating blind spots around where AI is being used and what information it can access.

Starting today, Sophos AI Defense is generally available, giving organizations the visibility and control to discover AI use, understand risk, apply guardrails, and protect sensitive information. Powered by Sophos Fusion, the Sophos AI-Native Cybersecurity Defense System, it brings AI security into the environment Sophos customers already use, rather than requiring another disconnected platform to manage. 

See AI. Control AI. Secure AI.

AI is increasingly embedded in the tools people use every day. That can create blind spots when employees adopt AI services that security teams do not know about or when AI functionality appears within applications already in use.

Sophos AI Defense helps bring that activity into view and gives security teams the context and controls to act:

  • See AI: Discover AI tools, agents, and workflows across your environment, including shadow AI.
  • Control AI: Apply practical guardrails for how AI can be used.
  • Secure AI: Protect sensitive information from AI-driven risk. 

Together, these capabilities help organizations move beyond simply knowing AI is being used to making informed decisions about how it should be used.

item.title: Building intent-based access control without reading minds
item.description:
In Minority Report, the Department of Precrime promised certainty. Three precognitives saw the future, the system picked the consensus, and police arrested people for murders they hadn't yet committed. The whole machine depended on one buried secret: sometimes the precogs disagreed, and the dissenting vision, the minority report, was quietly deleted. The system held together as long as the precogs agreed, but broke when it removed its own doubt.

A new wave of security products is reaching for the same capability. The pitch goes something like this: put a small AI model on every laptop, let it watch what people do across their apps, browsers, and AI tools the way a colleague sitting behind them would, understand what each person is trying to do, determine if they are malicious, and intervene before the damage is done. The same monitoring keeps a complete record of work, so an analyst can read what happened instead of piecing it together from scattered logs. The person might be an employee pasting sensitive data into an unapproved AI assistant, an outsider logged in with stolen credentials, or someone following a scammer's instructions to hand over remote control of their laptop. The watching part is now straightforward with local models. The design question is what a system should do with inference about intent that won’t always be correct.

Strip away the architecture and the pitch makes three promises: catch a risky action in time to stop it, tell it apart from normal work without burying analysts in alerts, and make whatever gets flagged quick to investigate. Useful intent-based access control can be built today by combining contextual inference with explicit policy and enforcement at sensitive actions. The research supports reconstructing what happened after the fact, scoring how well an action fits a person's job, and adding friction at the moment of risk. Recognizing someone's immediate goal while they're still pursuing it is less settled, and reliably separating malicious from benign motives in ordinary work is a challenge. So working systems test something more concrete: how well an action fits the person's job, how unusual it is for them, or which objective on a short list it matches. Each test trades false alarms for misses differently, and each leaves a gap an imitator can hide in, which is why the design around the test matters as much as the test itself. We’ll start with what a local model can read from the screen, move through the tests from most to least concrete, take the case where the intent belongs to someone else, and finish with how the tests combine into access control.

What a local model can read from the screen

Reconstructing what someone did on their screen already works surprisingly well. Cohen et al. split the job in two. A small model first summarizes each step of a short UI trajectory, using screenshots and action records to capture what was on screen and what the user did, and a second fine-tuned model infers the goal from those summaries. With Gemini Flash 8B as the small model, that decomposed pipeline inferred the user's goal about as well as Gemini 1.5 Pro, a model that cost more than 30 times as much per token. Jiang et al.'s task-induction method handles an earlier step, sorting interleaved computer-use traces back into their original tasks with near-perfect agreement.

Both results are retrospective. Each settles its answer after the last interaction, which suits post-incident response but doesn't establish how reliably a goal can be identified while someone is still pursuing it.

Established endpoint vendors and newer products alike are building around small, specialized models that make decisions in real time, in some cases directly on the device. Many rely mainly on structured events such as clipboard copies, file access, browser content, data lineage, and a baseline of each person's normal work. Some capture screenshots around an incident as evidence rather than continuously interpreting the screen, and that’s a reasonable choice: evidence that makes an alert quick to check lowers the cost of every false alarm. Logins, file access, process launches, and payment events arrive already labeled, so there's little left to summarize, and none of the studies reviewed here measures the added security value of reading the screen on top of those event streams.

The harder problem is inferring the goal mid-session from only the evidence available so far. GUIDE, a CVPR 2026 benchmark built from 67.5 hours of novice users working in apps like Photoshop and Excel, took a first step. It cut clips averaging about 25 seconds off at 25%, 50%, and 75% and asked models to pick the user's immediate goal from four options. With a quarter of the clip, the best model in this partial-clip experiment picked correctly about half the time, rising to about two thirds with the full clip, where random guessing gets 25%. Even with the overall task and possible immediate goals supplied, models frequently chose the wrong one. The researchers used users’ spoken explanations to establish the answers, but some intent was not recoverable from the screen alone.

Even a perfect, instant description settles nothing by itself. "Copying the customer list into a personal email draft" fits a sales rep finishing work at home as well as a sales rep leaving for a competitor. To act, a system has to determine if that is one of a myriad of benign goals or an example of rare malicious intent.

Job fit as the primary signal

The most concrete test asks whether an action fits its context. Google's Facade, which has monitored employee access to documents, databases, and internal services since 2018, is trained on unlabeled historical activity rather than known attacks and scores each access by how well it matches what the system knows about the person and the resource, such as their role, team, and recent work. Nobody has to write a menu of goals, and its authors report an event-level false-positive rate below 0.01% in their evaluation.

A small review queue comes with modest recall. In a red-team exercise, Google employees spent two weeks reaching for sensitive data outside their normal work using their own credentials. In a simulated daily review process, Facade retrieved three to four of the 15 attackers across five trained models at a budget of ten audits a day, a cost its authors call remarkably low for a company of more than 100,000 employees.

Its authors are explicit about the blind spot. Facade can't detect malicious actions that are indistinguishable from everyday work, which makes it unsuitable for catching a rogue employee reading files that are relevant to their job.

Deviation needs a review budget

Most insider-threat research takes a less concrete route: learn each person's normal behavior and flag what departs from it. However, real deployments show how much ordinary deviation there is. When Erola et al. ran an insider-threat tool inside three multinational companies, deliberately broad configurations produced about 356 anomalous alerts a day at one organization and 3,713 at another. The team detected a staged insider scenario, but could not establish how much of the ordinary flagged behavior was genuinely malicious. The authors found that real behavior deviates far more than the synthetic data most research relies on.

Synthetic benchmarks yield flattering results. A review of 131 studies built on the CERT insider-threat datasets found that nearly half use a release with 70 malicious users among 1,000, and few report how many alerts an analyst would review to find them. 

Lateral-movement detectors show the same pattern. When Larroche re-ran Euler and Argus with all remote logins retained in the Los Alamos National Laboratory test period, both still scored about 98% AUC, which measures how often a random attack outranks a random normal login. However, with only about two labeled malicious events per million, average precision fell below 0.1% for both, compared with the 5% and 32% reported on the original, more heavily filtered test sets.

Deviation can also be manipulated. Goyal et al. padded attacks with ordinary activity sampled from the target system, and reported 100% evasion against five detectors in their main public-dataset experiments, without changing the malicious payload.

Named objectives for known stories

Candidate-based goal recognition methods rank goals that someone already wrote down, and building that menu for an open-ended desktop session, where the user might be doing anything from editing a quarterly report to exfiltrating a database, is a problem they don't take on. Commercial products sidestep it by shrinking the menu to a few risk labels or policy categories. Screen-reading systems like Cohen's skip the menu by writing the intent in their own words, which creates a different problem. A security tool would still have to decide whether a free-text guess like "export the customer list" is malicious.

A detour can mean a hidden goal, or someone who is lost, rushed, or trying a fix that didn't work. Telling those apart starts with noticing the confusion, and current vision models often don't. In GUIDE's screen recordings of real novice users, the reported confusion matrix correctly classified only 7% of frustration clips and 4% of debugging clips. Most of those moments were labeled as confident work or deliberate exploration, reading repeated clicks, undos, and hesitation as purposeful progress. A security tool that reads struggle as purpose could see more intent in a detour than is really there.

Products go one step further and assign threat categories: malicious, careless, or compromised. The promise is a proportional response, coaching for the careless employee and an investigation for the malicious one, but those labels mix intent, behavior, and who controls the account. Distinguishing malicious motives from benign ones is harder than recognizing the immediate goal, and the evidence that would settle it may not be on the endpoint when the action happens. Facade deliberately avoids these labels. Its threat model treats a rogue employee and an employee whose stolen credentials someone else is using as the same case, because both look unusual for that person. 

Named-objective detectors turn motives and risk factors into stories. A recent review of insider-threat psychology discusses financial pressure, workplace grievances, and ideology, alongside a separate category of accidental or negligent harm. In DARPA's insider-threat program, Senator et al. built a detector for each of several such stories, including the saboteur, the fraudster, the careless user, and the employee walking off with intellectual property, and ran them over two months of monitored computer activity from about 5,500 employees, with red-team scenarios inserted into real users' records. The best of them, built for the leader of a small group stealing intellectual property, placed 6 red-team user-days in its October top 50, but in September it ignored 33 of 98 red-team user-days because they didn't fit the story. A named objective is a bet that the attacker will follow a story written in advance. Behavior outside that story can be missed, and an adaptive attacker has a reason to exploit the gap. This study did not test that deliberate evasion.

Friction when the intent belongs to someone else

Some intent doesn't belong to the person at the keyboard at all. A customer coached by a scammer over the phone can log in from their own device, pass authentication, and authorize the payment themselves, leaving familiar signs of account takeover absent. Dhama's theoretical study formalizes a limiting case: if scam and legitimate payments have identical observable feature distributions, a transaction-only detector cannot distinguish between them. The paper argues for adding session context and acknowledges clues in amounts, recipients, and timing.

Scam detection may be where reading the screen adds the most. A scam in progress can leave traces a payment record never sees, such as a remote-access tool running during a banking session or a chat window dictating the payee. ORACLE reads app usage and summarized screen content to warn before a scam completes, but it was tested on synthesized trajectories, so whether it catches live scams at a false-alarm rate a bank could live with is still open.

Friction at the moment of payment can help even without detection. In a field test on Alipay, the better-performing redesigned warning reduced the fraud-case rate among payments already flagged as risky from 0.24% to 0.13%. Both redesigned warnings retained reported pass rates above 90%.

However, scammers do adapt to friction. The UK's payment regulator reported fraudsters coaching victims to ignore warnings that a payee's name didn't match the account, sometimes by explaining that a new "safe account" had been set up that couldn't match yet.

Keep the minority report

For prevention, knowing the goal only helps if you learn it while there's still time to act. Products that promise to stop an action before it completes mostly act at the final step, such as the upload, with a warning, a request for justification, masking, or a block.

When the test at that step can't settle the question, the system can still choose to ask. Ren et al.'s KnowNo shows one way to decide when to ask. A language model reads a text description of the scene and proposes possible next actions for a robot, and KnowNo keeps every option that scores at or above a cutoff calibrated on held-out example tasks. If exactly one option survives, the robot acts. Otherwise it seeks human help, halting if the correct action is absent from the set. 

That's the minority report. When more than one option survives, the system is telling you it has a dissenting prediction. The movie deleted that signal to maintain the illusion of certainty. The research keeps it and uses it to decide when a human should weigh in. Jev's Paradox argued that confidence becomes operationally useful once it drives a decision policy.

Asking is already shipping in commercial products, several of which show a justification prompt or coaching message when intent is unclear. A question costs far less than a premature block, so the system can act on uncertain cases without paying the full price of a false alarm.

How the tests combine into access control

Each test in this piece fails differently, which is the argument for stacking them. Explicit policy sits at the sensitive action, such as the upload, the share, the payment, or the remote-access session, and decides what is permitted at all. Job-fit scoring of the kind Facade uses ranks what's left, because its reported false-positive rate is below 0.01% and it needs no menu of goals. Deviation from a person's baseline becomes an input to that score, so an unusual but plausible day raises a rank without producing an alert of its own. Named stories cover the few patterns worth writing down in advance, such as a departing employee staging files or a remote-access tool running while someone approves a payment, where a narrow detector gets high lift on the pattern it was written for and leaves the rest to the other layers.

When the combined evidence still leaves more than one plausible reading, the system keeps the minority report. A calibrated set of interpretations decides between acting, asking, and escalating. One surviving interpretation lets policy proceed or block. Several surviving interpretations trigger a justification prompt, step-up verification, or a short hold, and the session evidence travels with that decision to an analyst. Answers to those prompts go to the analyst as evidence, since the person most motivated to explain an action is the one the system can least take at their word.

The scoreboard has to reflect base rates. The numbers that matter are attackers caught at a fixed number of reviews per day, average precision against the full benign background, and how often legitimate work gets interrupted, because those are the costs a team actually feels. Red-team exercises should include imitation, padding malicious actions with ordinary activity the way Goyal et al. did, so the evaluation measures how the system handles an attacker who has read its filters.

Deployment can begin with a narrow workflow, such as sending customer data to an external AI service. Contextual scoring runs in observation mode first, measuring attacks caught within a fixed review budget and how often legitimate work would be interrupted. Clear policy violations can support immediate enforcement. Responses that depend on inferred intent expand as evaluation shows which interventions prevent harm at an acceptable cost to ordinary work.

The imitation failures this piece describes are documented blind spots, but how often they occur in real deployments and how well these tests hold up against adaptive attackers remain largely unmeasured. For security, deception is the norm, and it hides among base rates where approximately everything is benign.

Precrime fell to Lamar Burgess, the man who built it. He knew the system threw out repeated visions as echoes, so he staged a murder to look like one. He is the imitator every section of this piece warned about: an adversary who learns what the test treats as normal, whether that's a job-relevant file, an ordinary session, or a story the detector wasn't built for, and hides inside it. The best model keeps the minority report. When the test can't settle the question, it asks the user, waits, introduces friction, or flags the ambiguity for an analyst, on the assumption that the people who know its filters best are the ones most likely to use them.

For a human user, a security tool usually has to infer the task as well as judge the action. Whereas with an AI agent, the goal arrives in writing, but so does the attack, and an injected instruction can make sabotage look like progress. That makes agents the place where intent-based access control can be most precise, because every action can be checked against the stated task. The next piece looks at what it takes to hold an agent to that task.

Research and blogging assistance provided by Hermes, an AI Assistant. Its deviations from the outline were confusion, not concealment, but it understands why the distinction is hard to make from the outside.

item.title: AI governance needs more than a policy document
item.description:
AI tools have made it remarkably easy for a company to expose its own data:  

  • An employee pastes a customer list into a chatbot to reformat it. 
  • A developer drops proprietary code into an assistant to debug it. 
  • Someone connects a new AI product to their work account to save a few hours a week. 

None of these actions seem malicious, but each one moves sensitive information somewhere the security team cannot see. 

This new era of "move fast and break things”, a phrase famously coined by Mark Zuckerberg in the early Facebook days, benefits attackers. Company data now flows through more places, more third parties, and more delegated credentials. 

Shadow AI is already widespread:

  • 82% of organizations have discovered at least one AI tool or workflow that security and IT did not know existed.
  • 90% of IT leaders say they are concerned about shadow AI from a privacy and security standpoint.

Organizations know this is a problem and will enact an AI policy to educate employees about acceptable AI use and satisfy compliance requirements. The assumption is that if employees know the rules, they will follow them. Unfortunately, governance does not work that way.  

An policy document and employee training are just the beginning of an AI governance strategy. AI policy only works when it’s backed by visibility and technical controls enforced within user workflows.

A real-world shadow AI-driven incident

In April 2026, Vercel disclosed that an attacker had reached internal systems through a third-party AI tool. Here’s what happened:

An employee signed up for a consumer AI product using their corporate Google Workspace account.

  • That employee granted broad permissions during self-service signup.
  • That vendor was breached months later.
  • The attacker used the stolen OAuth token to take over the Workspace account and reach sensitive company environments.

The risk wasn't the AI tool itself. It was the absence of controls around how it connected to corporate accounts.

The problem: Policies buckle under delivery pressure

The instinct after an incident like this is to reinforce policy more frequently. But the evidence tells a different story:

  • Employees intentionally circumvent policy: A Gartner survey of 1,310 employees found that 69% had bypassed their organization's cybersecurity guidance in the previous 12 months, and 74% said they would be willing to bypass it if doing so helped them or their team hit a business objective. 
  • Employees often forget what training covers: Two large studies on anti-phishing training, one at UC San Diego Health with more than 19,500 employees and a reproduction at a US fintech firm with over 12,500, found that training barely changed whether people clicked on phishing emails.

IT operations teams run into these same issues when trying to get software engineers to follow written security requirements. Delivery pressure for these engineers would override following policies all the time.  

AI adoption follows the same pattern. When policy becomes a barrier to productivity, productivity will win.  

The fix: Encoding policies in a “paved road” 

What eventually worked in the IT operations field was encoding the safe path into the tooling developers already used. Jason Chan, the former VP of Information Security at Netflix, popularized the shorthand that stuck: paved roads and guardrails, not gates.  

While a gate is effective at stopping something in the moment, it can often motivate people to find an unsafe, unmonitored route to an unsafe action (like shadow AI). A guardrail is better because it still acts as a technically enforced boundary, but it also shows users an alternative path that’s safer. 

Successfully encoding AI governance policies starts with discovering those initial unsafe, unmonitored routes and understanding the user needs that created them. 

The first step is always discovery 

You cannot govern what you cannot see, so effective AI governance begins with visibility. However, the harsh truth is that many organizations still don’t know which AI tools employees use, what data is being shared, or where that data ends up. You can't apply a control to activity you haven't seen, so the first step is to shine a light on the AI happening in the shadows and use that data to inform your governance strategy.

Discovery has to cross boundaries because the activity does. The three main signals to start with are:

  • Browser sessions
  • Local device processes
  • Network calls (especially from unmanaged devices)

Once AI agents are being used frequently in your organization, delegated credentials to those agents are a fourth signal you’ll need to follow.  

Your AI inventory is wider than most policies assume since risk comes from more than just chatbots. You also need to track: 

  • Various types of AI applications
  • AI features shipped into SaaS applications your organization has already approved
  • Autonomous AI agents

You’ll need to scan for these AI inventory items continuously, then aggregate the data in the same dashboards and reports your IT or security operations team opens every day. Ideally, that single view includes: 

  • AI usage
  • Risk scoring
  • Policy status
  • Recommended actions 

Resist solutions that put findings in a separate console or outside established incident workflows. AI policy violations need to be visible in the main view that is frequently checked so they can be prioritized and investigated like any other security signal. 

Lastly, the ongoing discovery function should include a requirements-building function. Every unsanctioned action in your discovery report marks a place where the approved path didn’t meet user needs. Look for patterns and talk with AI users to compile a list of guardrail-design inputs rather than a list of offenders. 

How to effectively enforce AI policy 

The most common mistake in AI enforcement is treating it as binary: block or allow. But blocking too much without any recourse is the fastest way to push usage onto personal devices and personal accounts, where you have no visibility at all. In practice, most decisions should fall into three states, rather than two: 

  • Allow approved tools for defined users and groups.
  • Warn when something carries policy or risk concerns, offer other options.
  • Block what should not happen under any circumstance, redirect to other options.

The warn tier can be a user-facing message at the moment of action, a notification to an administrator, or both. It gives organizations visibility and coaching opportunities without immediately disrupting work, and it helps security teams guide behavior while evaluating new tools and emerging use cases. 

The block tier requires some nuance as well. When a block is applied, explain why. Employees are more likely to follow policy when they understand what triggered the action and what approved alternatives exist. 

IT and security teams should work with employees on new tools. Apply a safe proof of concept approach, evaluate the risks, and determine whether a tool can be adopted safely rather than simply maintaining a growing list of blocked applications. The answer to AI uncertainty is adaptability, not paralysis. 

Three control points: what each one covers 

Effective AI governance typically requires visibility and control across three key control points. They’re the same three surfaces that the discovery function focuses on: 

Control pointWhat it observesWhat it can enforce
Endpoint detection and controls 
  • General web activity
  • Process activity
  • User and device context
Tool and application access by user and group, including local agents and desktop AI clients. 
Network/Firewall 
  • AI service traffic
  • Non-browser activity
  • Unmanaged device activity
Service-level access, including paths that never touch a managed browser or a managed endpoint. 
Secure browser and workspace protection 
  • AI tool usage on the web
  • Prompt and upload activity
Uploads, downloads, copy and paste, and screen captures inside a managed browser. 

User identity and session context are also critical signals for evaluating AI activity. Many modern incidents begin with the compromise or misuse of legitimate credentials rather than malware. The Vercel breach demonstrates how quickly a trusted identity can become the starting point for a larger security event. 

One policy in one place 

Everything in your AI governance program, from the discovery inventory to the policy definitions, controls, and enforcement logs, should be visible and manageable through a shared operational view. No switching between disconnected consoles. 

When visibility and controls live together, organizations can move more quickly from detection to action, maintain more consistent policies, and provide a single source of truth for monitoring, investigation, and enforcement. 

What building the AI governance “paved road” looks like in practice 

When an unknown or unapproved AI tool is discovered, organizations should follow this sequence: 

  1. Detect: Signals from the endpoint, the network, and the browser surface the activity.
  2. Classify: A service nobody recognizes lands in a review queue. Your preference may be to block by default with a message explaining that the tool needs to be evaluated.
  3. Assess: Evaluate on identity, permissions, geography, data access, and behavior, not on the tool's name alone.
  4. Decide: Set an allow, warn, or block enforcement policy in your security system, scoped to the users and groups it applies to.
  5. Enforce: The next time an employee reaches for that service, apply the decision at the moment of use on whichever control point the activity crosses.
  6. Redirect: If the policy is to block this service, include a message with a named alternative and a visible route to request an exception.
  7. Route: Send the event into the detection and investigation workflows the team already runs, so an enforcement event can become an investigation when it needs to be.

Many organizations are still building capabilities across the early stages of this process. Effective AI governance strategy requires all seven.  

AI visibility to AI control and protection flow. 

Make the wrong thing hard and the right thing easy 

Boards, cyber insurers, regulators, and auditors increasingly expect the same level of visibility into AI usage, risks, and policy compliance that they demand across the rest of the security program.  

Instead of scrambling to assemble that evidence when questions arise, organizations should be able to quickly demonstrate what happened, which policies applied, and how those policies were enforced during a defined time period. 

An effective AI governance strategy relies on two key enforcement best practices:  

  • Make it difficult to do the damaging thing, through blocks applied where the activity actually happens. 
  • Make it easy to do the safe thing, through: 
    • Warnings that explain themselves
    • Redirects to approved alternatives
    • An exception path people can find

The written policy defines the rule. The control is what makes the rule true. 

The key to effective AI governance is applying visibility and enforcement through the control points organizations already operate across endpoints, network, and browser layers. Most dedicated AI security platforms require significant resources to deploy and manage while also adding one more standalone console. If AI governance data ends up somewhere your team does not already look, it will not get looked at. 

That is the thinking behind Sophos AI Defense. It helps organizations see AI, control AI, and secure AI using the security controls they already operate across endpoints, networks, browsers, and managed detection and response. Rather than introducing another standalone tool or console, it brings AI visibility, policy enforcement, and protection into the cybersecurity operations teams already use every day.

  • Sophos AI Defense: How visibility, control, and protection fit together across AI usage.
  • Building trust in the AI era: A broader look at securing AI adoption.

item.title: Show, don’t tell: Sophos AI at CAMLIS
item.description:
For the fourth year running, Sophos AI will share new research at the Conference on Applied Machine Learning in Information Security (CAMLIS). On October 23, Senior AI/ML Engineer Tamás Nyiri will lead a poster session entitled “Show, Don’t Tell: Calibrating Agentic SOC Analysts via Hierarchical Evidence Graphs.”

This research turns traces used in agentic investigations into features for a traditional ML model, which helps calibrate the agent’s verdicts and flag the cases it most likely got wrong.

A matter of fact

SOCs increasingly use AI agents to investigate alerts. Those agents extract entities and context connected to alerts, plan investigation steps, query tools, and produce reports containing final verdict.

While such agents can save analysts time, they can also fail in both predictable and surprising ways. An agent may treat a failed or missing check as evidence that nothing is wrong, link events simply because they happened close together, judge a legitimate installer or developer tool by its behavior alone, or close a case prematurely. These mistakes can be hard to spot, especially since reports tend to tell a confident story, while the evidence is buried in a long investigation trace.

Motivated by this challenge, Tamás developed an approach that makes an investigation agent show its evidence. First, the investigation steps are converted into a ‘fact graph,’ with the agent’s report and verdict withheld. Structured trace fields are parsed, while an LLM extracts meaning from free text under a fixed schema. The graph records what was observed, which tool calls failed, and how entities relate to one another. It also infers what is missing, such as unexamined alternative explanations and unqueried sources.

The fact graph is useful on its own, but here it serves as a building block for three evidence views:

  • Coverage: were the necessary checks actually run?
  • Context: do events link to the right entity, and is there a benign explanation?
  • Readiness: does the evidence justify a decision?

Features from these views feed a simple supervised model that estimates how likely a senior reviewer is to disagree with the agent’s verdict.

Show me the results

The training labels come from a two-stage human review. First, an analyst examines each agent investigation and gives a verdict; a senior analyst then reviews both and sets the final verdict, which serves as ground truth. The model is a regularized logistic regression, fit separately for three yes/no questions:

  1. Is the investigation conclusive?
  2. Is the initial alert a true positive
  3. Is the underlying content malicious in nature?

Alongside the evidence features, the model uses the agent’s verdict as a prior, based on how often reviewers agreed with that verdict in the training cases. This is necessary because labeling is costly and, at this training size, overfitting is unavoidable. Each of the 314 cases is scored by a model trained on the other 313 (leave-one-out cross-validation), so no case contributes to its own score.

The research is still at the proof-of-concept stage, with many improvements planned, but even this simple version shows an encouraging signal. Ranking cases by the model’s disagreement score brought agent errors to the front of the review queue. The senior reviewer overturned the agent’s verdict in 25% of all cases, but in 65% of the 20 highest-scoring cases: roughly 2.6 times the base rate.

During the session, Tamás will walk through the methodology, an example fact graph from a real case, and the lessons learned along the way.

If you’re attending CAMLIS, feel free to stop by Tamás’ poster to discuss your thoughts on this emerging research direction – and keep an eye out for more details of this approach in the near future.

But more recent incidents show how far beyond “email only” these intrusions can extend once an attacker gains control of a cloud identity.

In a recent case investigated by the Sophos X-Ops Incident Response team, a threat actor used voice phishing (vishing) and self-service password reset (SSPR) abuse to take over a Microsoft 365 account, establish a Primary Refresh Token (PRT)-backed device session, and pivot into multiple SaaS platforms. Rather than stopping at mailbox access, the actor treated the compromised identity as a springboard into the target’s broader SaaS estate.

Post-compromise activity was identified from a single compromised user account and included Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, access to email and SharePoint content including the download of nearly 100,000 documents, access to Salesforce, and a confirmed user-table export from ServiceNow of approximately 2,500 records. 

The Sophos X-Ops Incident Response team works with customers who have not previously purchased other Sophos offerings such as XDR. At the end of this writeup, we briefly cover the proactive, reactive, and behavioral protections available from Sophos via our other service offerings.

Initial access: SSPR abuse enabled by vishing

The compromise began with self-service password reset (SSPR) abuse. After several employees reported receiving suspicious phone calls from a suspected threat actor, the targeted organization sent a company-wide email warning users of the attack. However, one user had already unknowingly been compromised prior to the issuance of the emailed warning. The affected user later reported that the threat actor called by phone, impersonated help desk personnel, and convinced the user to provide the SMS-based MFA verification code needed to complete the reset flow.

Telemetry shows that an earlier SSPR initiation occurred from a geographically anomalous IP address the day before the confirmed vishing event. It is not clear whether that earlier attempt was directly related, but it may represent precursor probing or an unsuccessful attempt to validate the account. The confirmed compromise occurred when the actor initiated another SSPR flow from a different attacker-controlled IP, completed SMS verification, and successfully reset the user’s password.

This initial access method is important because it bypassed the need for a phishing page, malware, or an OAuth consent prompt. The user’s participation in a legitimate account recovery workflow was enough to hand over control of the identity.

From password reset to token-backed session

Within minutes of the successful password reset, the actor went beyond simple sign-in activity and established a device-backed cloud session.

The sequence included:

  • Entra ID registration of a new Windows device
  • successful use of a Primary Refresh Token
  • subsequent Microsoft Edge authentication using that token-backed device context

The actor established a persistent authenticated session tied to a newly registered Entra ID device, which gave them a more durable foothold than a single password-based web login.

In the sign-in records reviewed during the investigation, later access to ServiceNow was recorded as SAML 2.0 authentication using a primary refresh token, with MFA listed as “Previously satisfied.” That combination strongly suggests the actor was leveraging an already-authenticated Microsoft cloud session to access federated downstream applications, rather than performing repeated fully interactive reauthentication for each platform.

Immediate post-compromise activity in Microsoft 365

After gaining access to the account, the actor signed in to My Apps, Microsoft Graph, and Salesforce. Logs indicate the threat actor accessed emails, downloaded SharePoint documents, and launched Microsoft Teams. Microsoft Graph was used for initial reconnaissance, and over the course of the next day the actor began to sign in to additional applications, including ServiceNow.

This is not extraordinary behavior for a modern attacker. Once a threat actor has a valid session in the identity provider, they can enumerate accessible resources and pivot into downstream services. Mandiant’s reporting on recent GOLD CRYSTAL (ShinyHunters) linked and adjacent SaaS extortion activity has described this exact operational shift, where vishing and credential harvesting are used to obtain SSO access and then fan out into cloud applications for reconnaissance and data theft.

Structured Graph API reconnaissance

Sophos’s analysis of logs from GraphApiAuditEvents from Microsoft Defender identified evidence the threat actor’s activity included Graph API-driven reconnaissance queries consistent with:

  • Validating user context and licensing
  • Retrieving organization metadata
  • Enumerating tenant relationships
  • Mapping directory roles and effective permissions
  • Enumerating enterprise applications and service principals
  • Identifying verified tenant domains
  • Enumerating individual users and larger sets of directory objects

Examples of the query patterns documented during analysis included the following:

  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/me/licenseDetails
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/organization
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/beta/tenantRelationships/getResourceTenants?$select=tenantId
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/beta/users/{id}/roleManagement/directory/transitiveRoleAssignments?$count=true
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/beta/users/{id}/ownedObjects/Microsoft[.]graph[.]ServicePrincipal?$top=999
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/domains
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/sites
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/users/{UPN}?$select=userPrincipalName
  • hxxps[://]graph[.]microsoft[.]com/v1[.]0/users/$count 

Impact

The primary impact of the incident involved access to email and SharePoint data.

Sophos’s analysis of Microsoft’s Unified Audit Logs identified:

  • Over 100 unique mail items accessed across the compromised user’s mailbox and multiple shared mailboxes to which they had access
  • Approximately 100,000 unique SharePoint files downloaded

Access to emails is commonly the primary focus of BEC incidents, but this case shows how valuable a target SharePoint can be.

The threat actor accessed a relatively small number of mail items compared to the SharePoint files downloaded. A review of the subject lines of the emails accessed by the threat actor revealed a search pattern for messages related to account or credential related messages, customer information, internal organizational/team structure, and workflow approval-style emails. One of the messages reviewed by the actor was the organization's own vishing-awareness notification; that same message was subsequently deleted from the mailbox, demonstrating that the actor read and confirmed the organization was aware of the campaign before suppressing it from the compromised user's view.

For SharePoint, logs for SearchQueryInitiatedSharePoint indicate the threat actor searched for key terms with an apparent intent of identifying credentials, Personally Identifiable Information (PII), and information about product development and customers. Notably, four of the recovered queries, including several misspelled variants, targeted the organization's identity verification vendor by name, suggesting the actor either had prior knowledge of which MFA platform was in use or was specifically searching for documentation that might support a bypass.

A sample of keywords searched by the threat actor in this attack includes:

  • Salesforce
  • IT
  • Sales
  • Aws
  • NDA
  • Contracts
  • Login
  • Cred
  • Engineering
  • Customers
  • Jira
  • SSN
  • Contacts
  • Password
  • VPN
  • SSH 

Downstream SaaS pivot #1: Salesforce

The actor also pivoted into Salesforce using federated sign-in.

Entra sign-in telemetry showed multiple successful SAML-based accesses to Salesforce shortly after the attacker established the Microsoft cloud session. The reviewed Salesforce logs support the conclusion that the actor successfully accessed Salesforce, but the evidence reviewed in this case did not show large-scale CRM data extraction.

Salesforce logs showed a “SuspiciousActivity” event followed by successful execution of “FreezeUser” and “SendEmail”, indicating that Salesforce's automated anomaly-detection containment triggered, freezing the account and notifying the customer's Salesforce administrator.

Downstream SaaS pivot #2: ServiceNow

The largest non-Microsoft impact in this case came from attacker access to ServiceNow.

Entra telemetry showed a successful federated sign-in to the organization’s ServiceNow tenant. Subsequent ServiceNow logs from the same user context showed:

  • A successful login and session establishment
  • Navigation through dashboard views
  • Repeated access to the sys_user list view
  • Export activity targeting sys_user
  • Read access to the generated attachment sys_user.csv

Related export metadata indicated that the resulting CSV contained approximately 2,500 records.

The sys_user table that was targeted stores a record of everyone who logs in or interacts with ServiceNow and can include details such as name, email, phone number, roles, department, and manager. The presence of specific fields depends on the organization’s configuration settings. 

The information gathered from this would give the threat actor insight into:

  • Who exists in the platform
  • How user accounts are structured
  • How the organization is modeled

Combined with the contact information listed there, this information could be sold or used to conduct additional, more convincing social engineering attacks. In this case, the organization continued to receive numerous phishing and vishing attempts which may have utilized such information.

Notably, the same session later touched the CMDB [Configuration Management Database] Computer (cmdb_ci_computer) list view, indicating at least some additional browsing beyond the user directory. This can contain information about hardware inventory including computer names and operating systems. However, no evidence of export from that table was identified. 

Microsoft Teams access

Purview logs contained a TeamsSessionStarted operation performed by the threat actor, indicating Microsoft Teams was launched. Microsoft records events for activities such as message creation, edits, deletions, participant additions, and the creation of new chats or teams, but it does not audit the passive viewing of existing messages in chats and channels a user already has access to. This is a commonly overlooked gap. Threat actors can gather significant sensitive information through passive reconnaissance of Teams chats without leaving any audit trail of what was read.

Defense evasion and cleanup

The actor did not create inbox rules, forwarding rules, or new applications — a notable absence in a case that otherwise resembles modern BEC and SaaS intrusion playbooks.

Instead, the only observed cleanup behavior in Exchange was the deletion of two messages:

  • One warning users about active vishing attempts in the environment
  • One additional message of unknown content

That first deletion is particularly telling. The organization had already begun warning users about the scam calls, but the compromised user was kept from seeing that warning because the actor removed it from their mailbox.

Recommendations

This intrusion is a useful illustration that identity-centric attacks no longer stop at the mailbox. The recommendations below are scoped to the specific behaviors observed in this case and are prioritized by the leverage they would have given defenders against this exact intrusion path.

Harden the account recovery surface, not just sign-in

Phishing-resistant MFA is increasingly the default conversation for sign-in, but the same scrutiny rarely extends to recovery. In this case, the entire intrusion was unlocked because the SSPR flow accepted an SMS code the user handed over during a vishing call. 

For organizations not yet able to remove SMS and voice entirely from SSPR, several intermediate controls reduce exposure:

  • Prefer phishing-resistant factors (FIDO2 security keys, passkeys, Windows Hello for Business, certificate-based authentication) as the highest-priority registered method for recovery flows
  • Where SMS is retained, scope it tightly. Exclude administrative accounts, require explicit registration rather than directory-sourced phone numbers, and treat SSPR initiations from anonymizing infrastructure or unexpected geolocations as detection signals
  • Monitor SSPR flows for behavioral anomalies (rapid registration of a new device immediately after reset, geographic mismatch between SSPR initiation and recent legitimate sign-ins)
  • Pair technical controls with targeted user awareness. The vishing pretext in this case was specifically that "the help desk" needed an MFA code; users should be trained that legitimate help desk staff will never request an MFA or verification code by phone, and any such request should be reported

Treat device registration as a privileged operation

The pivot from "stolen password" to "durable cloud foothold" happened the moment the actor registered a new Windows device against the compromised identity. Once that device existed, PRT-backed sessions made every downstream pivot look routine. Defenders should:

  • Review device onboarding and enrollment processes. Confirm there are appropriate checks to verify both the user's identity and ownership of the device before enrollment is approved. Ensure enrolment is restricted to authorized device types and managed hardware where possible.
  • Alert on any new device registration within a short window of a password reset, MFA method change, or anomalous sign-in
  • Require MFA on device registration itself (not just on the sign-in that precedes it)
  • Pair device registration alerts with automated session revocation for the associated identity until a human verifies the registration is legitimate

Assume the blast radius is the whole SaaS estate

Once the actor held a valid identity, lateral movement happened through federation, not exploitation. Mail, SharePoint, Salesforce, and ServiceNow were all reachable through the same Microsoft cloud session, and the actor moved between them in a single afternoon. That means:

  • Containment cannot end at "reset the password." Effective containment requires revoking active sessions and refresh tokens across the identity provider and every federated SaaS platform the identity could reach
  • SaaS platforms with high-value identity or organizational data including ticketing, ITSM, and CRM systems should be added to the incident-response runbook alongside email and file-sharing systems
  • ServiceNow in particular warrants dedicated detection coverage. The sys_user and cmdb_ci_computer tables are high-value reconnaissance targets and bulk export from either is a strong investigative signal
  • Salesforce's automated anomaly containment (which triggered in this case and froze the actor's session) is a useful complementary control, but customers should validate that equivalent automated containment exists in their other federated SaaS platforms

Hunt and monitor for post-compromise reconnaissance, not just initial access

A lot of identity-compromise detection is front-loaded around the sign-in event itself. In this case, the most telling activity happened after the actor was already inside: structured Graph API enumeration, SharePoint keyword searches for credentials and PII, and federated SAML sign-ins to downstream SaaS. Defenders should build hunts for:

  • GraphApiAuditEvents activity consistent with directory, role, and service principal enumeration from a single user session
  • SearchQueryInitiatedSharePoint events containing terms like password, cred, aws, vpn, ssh, or the name of the organization's own identity or MFA vendor
  • MailItemsAccessed volume anomalies, particularly access to security-awareness and account-notification emails followed by their deletion
  • Federated SAML sign-ins to SaaS applications from sessions that have not previously accessed those applications, especially when MFA is satisfied by an existing token claim rather than an interactive prompt
  • Bulk export operations against identity, CMDB, and CRM tables in federated SaaS platforms

Sophos protections

The target of these attacks was not, prior to the events in this article, a Sophos customer. Sophos customers would have been protected from this series of events at various points, including:

Proactive rules

  • Sophos ITDR flags tenants for which SMS, voice call, and email OTP remain enabled as authentication methods, and for which SSPR for non-admins accepts a single method. These checks push account recovery away from verification codes that can be handed over during a vishing call.
  • Sophos ITDR flags tenants that do not block high-risk users or high-risk sign-ins, and checks whether geographic Conditional Access controls and trusted named locations are configured. Trusted locations give Entra ID Protection more context for risk calculation; these controls help with follow-on sign-ins when the source is out of region or scored as risky, rather than directly governing the SSPR flow.
  • Sophos ITDR flags tenants that do not protect the “Register or join devices” action with Conditional Access requiring MFA or block for all users, and tenants without policy protecting security-information registration. It also recommends defining trusted IP-based named locations, which customers can use as a signal when scoping registration from known corporate networks.
  • Sophos ITDR flags tenants that do not require compliant devices in Conditional Access, or do not enforce session controls such as sign-in frequency and non-persistent browser sessions on unmanaged devices. These controls reduce the durable access available to a freshly registered, unmanaged device.
  • Sophos ITDR flags tenants where administrators can still use SSPR through the authorization policy (check: “Prevent Weak Admin Authentication by Disabling Authorization Policy SSPR”).

Reactive rules

  • “Azure Device Registration and Unseen Login Property” correlates device registration with a login from an unseen IP, ASN or user agent within one hour. It matches this sequence closely, but is currently a research rule and does not alert. A separate alerting rule applies when unseen-IP sign-in is followed by security-info registration and a new Authenticator device, which this article does not confirm.
  • Sophos ITDR alerts on Azure CLI or PowerShell use by a user with no prior history. This could provide coverage if the Graph reconnaissance used one of those clients, but the investigation does not identify the client, so we should not claim that it would have fired. We do not currently have direct coverage here for general Graph directory, role or service-principal enumeration from a single session.
  • Sophos XDR alerts on “Unusual Login and File Download Behavior Detected from Single IP for a User,” correlating an anomalous login with mass SharePoint downloads from the same IP within one hour. A second alerting variant covers unusual login followed by downloads through a suspicious or non-standard client.

Behavioral signaling

  • Sophos identity analytics baseline IP address, ASN, country and user agent per user. Previously unseen values, including a switch to new attacker infrastructure, feed higher-confidence compromise correlations; “Multiple Unseen Countries for User” can also alert when the locations meet that condition.
  • Sophos identity analytics baseline application access and client properties such as user agent, IP, ASN and country. Previously unseen applications or client properties add context to post-compromise activity, but are supporting signals rather than proof of compromise by themselves.

Conclusion

No single step in this intrusion was novel. The actor reset a password, registered a device, used a refresh token, queried Graph, and signed into federated apps. Every one of those actions is a workflow Microsoft and the surrounding SaaS ecosystem designed to be frictionless for legitimate users. The novelty was in the assembly: a vishing call at the front end and a ServiceNow user-table export at the back end, with a fully sanctioned cloud session connecting them.

That is a harder problem for defenders. There is no malware to find, no exploit to patch, and no obviously malicious tool to block. The activity blends with normal use because, mechanically, it is normal use performed by the wrong person. Programs built around identity behavior, session lineage, and cross-SaaS correlation will see most of it.

For organizations still treating BEC as a mailbox problem, this case is a useful prompt to widen the scope. The mailbox is rarely the destination anymore; it is just the first room the attacker walks through.

The indicators of compromise associated with this attack will be made available on our GitHub.

Notably, the same session later touched the CMDB [Configuration Management Database] Computer (cmdb_ci_computer) list view, indicating at least some additional browsing beyond the user directory. This can contain information about hardware inventory including computer names and operating systems. However, no evidence of export from that table was identified. 

Microsoft Teams access

Purview logs contained a TeamsSessionStarted operation performed by the threat actor, indicating Microsoft Teams was launched. Microsoft records events for activities such as message creation, edits, deletions, participant additions, and the creation of new chats or teams, but it does not audit the passive viewing of existing messages in chats and channels a user already has access to. This is a commonly overlooked gap. Threat actors can gather significant sensitive information through passive reconnaissance of Teams chats without leaving any audit trail of what was read.

Defense evasion and cleanup

The actor did not create inbox rules, forwarding rules, or new applications — a notable absence in a case that otherwise resembles modern BEC and SaaS intrusion playbooks.

Instead, the only observed cleanup behavior in Exchange was the deletion of two messages:

  • One warning users about active vishing attempts in the environment
  • One additional message of unknown content

That first deletion is particularly telling. The organization had already begun warning users about the scam calls, but the compromised user was kept from seeing that warning because the actor removed it from their mailbox.

Recommendations

This intrusion is a useful illustration that identity-centric attacks no longer stop at the mailbox. The recommendations below are scoped to the specific behaviors observed in this case and are prioritized by the leverage they would have given defenders against this exact intrusion path.

Harden the account recovery surface, not just sign-in

Phishing-resistant MFA is increasingly the default conversation for sign-in, but the same scrutiny rarely extends to recovery. In this case, the entire intrusion was unlocked because the SSPR flow accepted an SMS code the user handed over during a vishing call. 

For organizations not yet able to remove SMS and voice entirely from SSPR, several intermediate controls reduce exposure:

  • Prefer phishing-resistant factors (FIDO2 security keys, passkeys, Windows Hello for Business, certificate-based authentication) as the highest-priority registered method for recovery flows
  • Where SMS is retained, scope it tightly. Exclude administrative accounts, require explicit registration rather than directory-sourced phone numbers, and treat SSPR initiations from anonymizing infrastructure or unexpected geolocations as detection signals
  • Monitor SSPR flows for behavioral anomalies (rapid registration of a new device immediately after reset, geographic mismatch between SSPR initiation and recent legitimate sign-ins)
  • Pair technical controls with targeted user awareness. The vishing pretext in this case was specifically that "the help desk" needed an MFA code; users should be trained that legitimate help desk staff will never request an MFA or verification code by phone, and any such request should be reported

Treat device registration as a privileged operation

The pivot from "stolen password" to "durable cloud foothold" happened the moment the actor registered a new Windows device against the compromised identity. Once that device existed, PRT-backed sessions made every downstream pivot look routine. Defenders should:

  • Review device onboarding and enrollment processes. Confirm there are appropriate checks to verify both the user's identity and ownership of the device before enrollment is approved. Ensure enrolment is restricted to authorized device types and managed hardware where possible.
  • Alert on any new device registration within a short window of a password reset, MFA method change, or anomalous sign-in
  • Require MFA on device registration itself (not just on the sign-in that precedes it)
  • Pair device registration alerts with automated session revocation for the associated identity until a human verifies the registration is legitimate

Assume the blast radius is the whole SaaS estate

Once the actor held a valid identity, lateral movement happened through federation, not exploitation. Mail, SharePoint, Salesforce, and ServiceNow were all reachable through the same Microsoft cloud session, and the actor moved between them in a single afternoon. That means:

  • Containment cannot end at "reset the password." Effective containment requires revoking active sessions and refresh tokens across the identity provider and every federated SaaS platform the identity could reach
  • SaaS platforms with high-value identity or organizational data including ticketing, ITSM, and CRM systems should be added to the incident-response runbook alongside email and file-sharing systems
  • ServiceNow in particular warrants dedicated detection coverage. The sys_user and cmdb_ci_computer tables are high-value reconnaissance targets and bulk export from either is a strong investigative signal
  • Salesforce's automated anomaly containment (which triggered in this case and froze the actor's session) is a useful complementary control, but customers should validate that equivalent automated containment exists in their other federated SaaS platforms

Hunt and monitor for post-compromise reconnaissance, not just initial access

A lot of identity-compromise detection is front-loaded around the sign-in event itself. In this case, the most telling activity happened after the actor was already inside: structured Graph API enumeration, SharePoint keyword searches for credentials and PII, and federated SAML sign-ins to downstream SaaS. Defenders should build hunts for:

  • GraphApiAuditEvents activity consistent with directory, role, and service principal enumeration from a single user session
  • SearchQueryInitiatedSharePoint events containing terms like password, cred, aws, vpn, ssh, or the name of the organization's own identity or MFA vendor
  • MailItemsAccessed volume anomalies, particularly access to security-awareness and account-notification emails followed by their deletion
  • Federated SAML sign-ins to SaaS applications from sessions that have not previously accessed those applications, especially when MFA is satisfied by an existing token claim rather than an interactive prompt
  • Bulk export operations against identity, CMDB, and CRM tables in federated SaaS platforms

Sophos protections

The target of these attacks was not, prior to the events in this article, a Sophos customer. Sophos customers would have been protected from this series of events at various points, including:

Proactive rules

  • Sophos ITDR flags tenants for which SMS, voice call, and email OTP remain enabled as authentication methods, and for which SSPR for non-admins accepts a single method. These checks push account recovery away from verification codes that can be handed over during a vishing call.
  • Sophos ITDR flags tenants that do not block high-risk users or high-risk sign-ins, and checks whether geographic Conditional Access controls and trusted named locations are configured. Trusted locations give Entra ID Protection more context for risk calculation; these controls help with follow-on sign-ins when the source is out of region or scored as risky, rather than directly governing the SSPR flow.
  • Sophos ITDR flags tenants that do not protect the “Register or join devices” action with Conditional Access requiring MFA or block for all users, and tenants without policy protecting security-information registration. It also recommends defining trusted IP-based named locations, which customers can use as a signal when scoping registration from known corporate networks.
  • Sophos ITDR flags tenants that do not require compliant devices in Conditional Access, or do not enforce session controls such as sign-in frequency and non-persistent browser sessions on unmanaged devices. These controls reduce the durable access available to a freshly registered, unmanaged device.
  • Sophos ITDR flags tenants where administrators can still use SSPR through the authorization policy (check: “Prevent Weak Admin Authentication by Disabling Authorization Policy SSPR”).

Reactive rules

  • “Azure Device Registration and Unseen Login Property” correlates device registration with a login from an unseen IP, ASN or user agent within one hour. It matches this sequence closely, but is currently a research rule and does not alert. A separate alerting rule applies when unseen-IP sign-in is followed by security-info registration and a new Authenticator device, which this article does not confirm.
  • Sophos ITDR alerts on Azure CLI or PowerShell use by a user with no prior history. This could provide coverage if the Graph reconnaissance used one of those clients, but the investigation does not identify the client, so we should not claim that it would have fired. We do not currently have direct coverage here for general Graph directory, role or service-principal enumeration from a single session.
  • Sophos XDR alerts on “Unusual Login and File Download Behavior Detected from Single IP for a User,” correlating an anomalous login with mass SharePoint downloads from the same IP within one hour. A second alerting variant covers unusual login followed by downloads through a suspicious or non-standard client.

Behavioral signaling

  • Sophos identity analytics baseline IP address, ASN, country and user agent per user. Previously unseen values, including a switch to new attacker infrastructure, feed higher-confidence compromise correlations; “Multiple Unseen Countries for User” can also alert when the locations meet that condition.
  • Sophos identity analytics baseline application access and client properties such as user agent, IP, ASN and country. Previously unseen applications or client properties add context to post-compromise activity, but are supporting signals rather than proof of compromise by themselves.

Conclusion

No single step in this intrusion was novel. The actor reset a password, registered a device, used a refresh token, queried Graph, and signed into federated apps. Every one of those actions is a workflow Microsoft and the surrounding SaaS ecosystem designed to be frictionless for legitimate users. The novelty was in the assembly: a vishing call at the front end and a ServiceNow user-table export at the back end, with a fully sanctioned cloud session connecting them.

That is a harder problem for defenders. There is no malware to find, no exploit to patch, and no obviously malicious tool to block. The activity blends with normal use because, mechanically, it is normal use performed by the wrong person. Programs built around identity behavior, session lineage, and cross-SaaS correlation will see most of it.

For organizations still treating BEC as a mailbox problem, this case is a useful prompt to widen the scope. The mailbox is rarely the destination anymore; it is just the first room the attacker walks through.

item.title: ConnectWise Cloud Backup application abused in cross-tenant token sweep
item.description:
On October 15, 2026, Sophos X-Ops researchers identified a series of service principal sign-ins in which a threat actor authenticated as the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application (formerly SkyKick) and requested app-only Microsoft Graph tokens from customer Microsoft 365 tenants. The malicious scanning activity originated from a single virtual private server (VPS) and continued for about 96 minutes. X-Ops researchers found no evidence of hands-on-keyboard activity and assess with high confidence that the threat actor ran a script that enumerated a list of tenants that had consented to the application.

The sign-ins required no user password and no multi-factor authentication (MFA) because the threat actor authenticated with the application's own identity. This activity is consistent with abuse of a compromised vendor-held application credential. It is unclear how the credential was obtained or what the threat actor did with the obtained tokens.

ConnectWise published an advisory about the service interruption, as well as a technical investigation and remediation guide. The advisory notes that ConnectWise shut off Cloud Backup application access for partners and customers as a protective measure.;

Background

ConnectWise Cloud Backup is a Microsoft 365 product that operates through a multi-tenant Entra application. When a customer enables the product, they consent to the application in their tenant. This consent allows the vendor's application identity to request Microsoft Graph tokens for the tenant to read data for backup. A threat actor who obtains the application's credential can request the same tokens in every tenant that has granted consent.

Observed activity

X-Ops researchers observed the threat actor request one app-only Graph token for the Cloud Backup application in each targeted tenant. The reconnaissance began at 07:11 UTC on October 15, and the last observed scan was at 08:47 UTC. All requests originated from 144[.]172[.]64[.]128 and used the following User-Agents: Python-urllib/3.12 and python-requests/2.31.

Analysis revealed three characteristics that point to automated activity:

  • Tenants were accessed in strictly ascending tenant GUID order.
  • Requests were spaced one to six minutes apart.
  • The sweep included tenants with no active backup subscription, which suggests the threat actor worked from a full list of tenants that had consented to the application, including those that were no longer active backup customers.

As of this publication, there is no evidence that the application created new secrets, applications, consents, or role assignments in the reviewed tenants.

Recommendations

Organizations that use or have ever used ConnectWise Cloud Backup or SkyKick products should take the following actions:

  • Review Entra enterprise applications and remove consent for the applications that ConnectWise disabled.
  • Review Entra sign-in logs during the October 15-17 timeframe, specifically service principal sign-ins for the indicators that have been associated with this activity.
  • Review audit logs for new credentials, secrets, application registrations, consents, and role assignments made by these applications since October 13.
  • Retrieve Microsoft Graph activity logs for tenants with active backup, if available, to evaluate how issued tokens were used.
  • Follow the vendor's remediation guidance, including credential rotation steps.

Countermeasures and indicators

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this incident and will deliver detections and protections as available.

The indicators in Table 1 can be used to detect activity related to this threat. Note that IP addresses can be reallocated.
