item.title: BRONZE SANDCASTLE deploys modified Meterpreter shells
item.description:
Counter Threat Unit™ (CTU) and SophosLabs researchers investigated a cluster of incidents attributed to the BRONZE SANDCASTLE threat group. The most distinctive technical marker for BRONZE SANDCASTLE is its consistent use of Sandboxie DLL sideloading.

DLL sideloading details

Across multiple victims’ environments, legitimate Sandboxie executables were placed alongside a malicious sbiedll.dll file, causing the trusted application to load attacker-controlled code at runtime. This consistent pattern functions as a signature for the group, although the threat actors employ several other sideloading file combinations as well (see Table 1).

Legitimate fileMalicious sideloaded DLL
SandboxieWUAU.exe (Sandboxie)sbiedll.dll
Start.exe (renamed Sandboxie executable)sbiedll.dll
javaw.exe (Java application)jli.dll
Krita.exe (Krita digital painting)Krita.dll
NvdaHelper.exe (NVDA NonVisual Desktop Access)NvdaHelperRemote.dll
Jcef_helper.exe (Java Chromium Embedded Framework Helper)Libcef.dll
Vmmap.exe (Sysinternals process memory analyzer)Version.dll
LineAppMgr.exe (LINE messaging application)msvcp140.dll
bginfo64.exe (Sysinternals utility that displays system information)snmpapi.dll

Table 1: DLL sideloading files used by BRONZE SANDCASTLE

The sideloaded DLLs typically read and execute payloads stored in encrypted config.ini files. This design minimizes static detection and allows operators to adjust behavior without replacing DLL binaries. Renamed legitimate executables are frequently used to blend into victims’ environments, with execution resulting in in-memory shellcode activity rather than additional disk artifacts. Figure 1 shows the components of a sample ZIP archive (aez.zip) on a compromised system: the clean loader (javaw.exe), the sideloaded DLL (jli.dll), and the file containing the encrypted payload (config.ini).

Figure 1: Sample DLL sideloading components deployed in a ZIP archive on a compromised system

The malicious DLL code implements a flattened control-flow dispatcher that obscures program logic by using a virtualized state machine instead of direct branches (see Figure 2).

Figure 2: Core sequence of the DLL’s code obfuscation

A state value indexes a per-state table, and a value from the table is passed through a custom bit-mixing routine using byte swapping, variable rotations, inversion, and negation. The result is used as an index into a jump table of code pointers, and execution continues via an indirect jump. Some indices intentionally resolve to fall-through locations, further complicating static analysis and obscuring the program’s true control flow.

Payload

The decrypted payload is a backdoor program. Once loaded and decoded by the DLL, config.ini superficially resembles a Windows executable in memory (see Figure 3).

Figure 3: Decoded config.ini file in memory

The file header is a position‑independent PE loader and execution stub, often referred to as a reflective loader. The payload exhibits structural similarities to stageless shellcode payloads such as those generated by the Metasploit Framework (MSF), including position-independent execution, manual PE validation, and in-memory loading of an embedded executable. However, several implementation details indicate that this loader is not a standard Metasploit artifact. In particular, the API resolution logic uses non-standard hashing and transformation routines rather than the well-known ROR13 algorithm used by Metasploit, and the codebase is significantly larger and more complex than typical MSF shellcode.

The analyzed samples also contain elements of the well-known COFFLoader project (see Figure 4). The use of standard APIs from this project suggests that the malware author employed a custom Beacon Object File (BOF) to create their own post-exploitation features.

Figure 4: COFFLoader elements observed in compromised systems’ memory

Additional in-memory strings associated with C++ function decorators demonstrate the data-stealing capabilities that BRONZE SANDCASTLE builds into its payload (see Figure 5).

Figure 5: In-memory strings from BRONZE SANDCASTLE's payload

Sophos analysts identified two versions of the payload: 1.1.5 and 1.1.7. Once running, the payload sends a structured JSON object with nested “info” block to its command and control (C2) server (see Figure 6). The following information is included in that block:

  • Host identifiers: hostname, username, GUID, domain
  • OS version (e.g.,10.0.19042)
  • Internal IP address
  • Public IP address
  • Process listing and metadata (PID, process name, execution method)
  • Working directory
  • Code page
  • CPU architecture
  • Implant start time
  • Implant type (server/client)

Figure 6: Formatted JSON info block in version 1.1.7

CTU™ researchers observed instances of the payload reaching out to legitimate websites such as file[.]io, gofile[.]io, ably[.]net, and ably[.]io, possibly to receive C2 tasking from the operators. Version 1.1.5 contacted C2 servers dc[.]cathaypacifice[.]com and net[.]dpworldto[.]com. Version 1.1.7 payloads have also been observed communicating with github[.]com repositories to download encrypted config files (see Figure 7).

Figure 7: Payload attempting to download a config file from GitHub

The GitHub repository (hxxps://api[.]github[.]com/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW) has little history, with only a few submissions (see Figure 8).

Figure 8: Overview page of LatonyCharnleyaW GitHub repo

The repository contained multiple files. Analysis suggested that the following files were likely encrypted config files: main.3ku8inqb.js.map, main.lhxjkkai.js.map, main.y8hnze7q.js.map, and README.md. There were also encrypted files with a .ts extension (see Figure 9) that may be implants used by the backdoor.

Figure 9: List of .ts files in the GitHub repository

After a payload is installed in a target environment, the threat actors use it to conduct common survey tasks such as executing Windows “net” commands to enumerate the local network and user accounts. The threat actors have also created Volume Shadow copies via vssadmin.exe prior to copying the Windows ntds.dit file. This Windows file is the central database file of Active Directory that contains user credentials, group policies, security settings, and domain configurations.

Victimology and links to China

CTU researchers have observed BRONZE SANDCASTLE targeting organizations in Asia and Africa, which is typical of several China-based threat groups, including BRONZE PRESIDENT and BRONZE ATLAS. Although the geographic targeting overlaps with that of these groups, the observed activity could not be reliably linked to either group and exhibited distinctive technical characteristics. CTU researchers consequently created the separate BRONZE SANDCASTLE designation to represent the group behind this activity.

CTU analysis of incidents between August 2025 and August 2026 revealed victims in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia, and likely also the Republic of Korea (see Figure 10).

Figure 10: Distribution of BRONZE SANDCASTLE victims in incidents between August 2025 and August 2026

Observations that the threat actors are most active in UTC+8 time (see Figure 11) reinforces attribution to a China-based threat group. The active hours align with the 996 working hour system that is particularly popular in China’s tech sector.

Figure 11: Heatmap of BRONZE SANDCASTLE activity by hour of the day

The details of the observed loaders and the novel Meterpreter-based payload appear to be specific to BRONZE SANDCASTLE.

Recommendations

Organizations at risk of targeting by China’s intelligence-gathering operations should familiarize themselves with BRONZE SANDCASTLE’s tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). The threat group predominantly uses encrypted payload and configuration files that are decoded at runtime, meaning that static file-based detections may be ineffective. Organizations should instead focus on behavioral indicators such as DLLs reading local files followed by immediate in-memory execution, which may indicate decoding and staging activity. Endpoint telemetry and memory-based detection are essential. Security teams should enable monitoring for reflective loading patterns, anomalous PE headers in memory, and processes exhibiting characteristics of position-independent shellcode execution.

Countermeasures and indicators

The following Sophos countermeasures relate to this threat:

  • ATK/Swrort-Y
  • ATK/ScLoad-W
  • ATK/ScLoad-X
  • ATK/ScLoad-Y
  • ATK/ScLoad-Z
  • Troj/Loader-JL
  • Troj/Loader-JP

Due to the large number of threat indicators, the full list is available in the SophosLabs GitHub repository.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Colin Cowie, Jordon Olness, and Morgan Demboski for their analysis and insight into this activity.

There were also encrypted files with a .ts extension (see Figure 9) that may be implants used by the backdoor.

Figure 9: List of .ts files in the GitHub repository

After a payload is installed in a target environment, the threat actors use it to conduct common survey tasks such as executing Windows “net” commands to enumerate the local network and user accounts. The threat actors have also created Volume Shadow copies via vssadmin.exe prior to copying the Windows ntds.dit file. This Windows file is the central database file of Active Directory that contains user credentials, group policies, security settings, and domain configurations.

Victimology and links to China

CTU researchers have observed BRONZE SANDCASTLE targeting organizations in Asia and Africa, which is typical of several China-based threat groups, including BRONZE PRESIDENT and BRONZE ATLAS. Although the geographic targeting overlaps with that of these groups, the observed activity could not be reliably linked to either group and exhibited distinctive technical characteristics. CTU researchers consequently created the separate BRONZE SANDCASTLE designation to represent the group behind this activity.

CTU analysis of incidents between August 2025 and August 2026 revealed victims in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia, and likely also the Republic of Korea (see Figure 10).

Figure 10: Distribution of BRONZE SANDCASTLE victims in incidents between August 2025 and August 2026

Observations that the threat actors are most active in UTC+8 time (see Figure 11) reinforces attribution to a China-based threat group. The active hours align with the 996 working hour system that is particularly popular in China’s tech sector.

Figure 11: Heatmap of BRONZE SANDCASTLE activity by hour of the day

The details of the observed loaders and the novel Meterpreter-based payload appear to be specific to BRONZE SANDCASTLE.

Recommendations

Organizations at risk of targeting by China’s intelligence-gathering operations should familiarize themselves with BRONZE SANDCASTLE’s tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). The threat group predominantly uses encrypted payload and configuration files that are decoded at runtime, meaning that static file-based detections may be ineffective. Organizations should instead focus on behavioral indicators such as DLLs reading local files followed by immediate in-memory execution, which may indicate decoding and staging activity. Endpoint telemetry and memory-based detection are essential. Security teams should enable monitoring for reflective loading patterns, anomalous PE headers in memory, and processes exhibiting characteristics of position-independent shellcode execution.

Countermeasures and indicators

The following Sophos countermeasures relate to this threat:

  • ATK/Swrort-Y
  • ATK/ScLoad-W
  • ATK/ScLoad-X
  • ATK/ScLoad-Y
  • ATK/ScLoad-Z
  • Troj/Loader-JL
  • Troj/Loader-JP

Due to the large number of threat indicators, the full list is available in the SophosLabs GitHub repository.

Thanks to Colin Cowie, Jordon Olness, and Morgan Demboski for their analysis and insight into this activity.

item.title: Why Incident Response Demand Will Grow Faster than Expected
item.description:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security operations specialists, sharing the expertise they use to strengthen our industry-leading Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service and defend customers against evolving AI-era threats.

A 20% growth forecast for cybersecurity talent sounds significant. I believe it understates what we are going to see in Incident Response. 

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 21% employment growth for information security analysts between 2025 and 2035. That projection applies to the broader information security profession, not specifically to Incident Response. Still, it gives us a useful benchmark. 

Based on what I am seeing and hearing across the industry, Incident Response demand could grow much faster. 

I attend security conferences where leaders from other firms openly say they are hiring Incident Response analysts. Our partners tell us they are hiring. DFIR firms we know are asking whether they can use Sophos to provide overflow support when their teams reach capacity. 

These are not isolated conversations. They are consistent signals from across the security ecosystem. 

Everyone is looking for more Incident Response capacity.

AI is giving attackers greater scale 

AI has changed what threat actors can accomplish with the people and resources they already have. 

Attackers still rely on many of the same techniques. They steal credentials, exploit vulnerabilities, use social engineering, move laterally, and target critical systems. What is changing is the speed and scale at which they can do it. 

The Sophos AI Security 2026 Report found that AI is compressing attack timelines rather than creating entirely new categories of attacks. It is enabling both attackers and defenders to move faster through familiar operations. 

That distinction is important. 

We do not need to wait for a fully autonomous AI attacker before treating this as a serious capacity problem. If AI helps an attacker research more targets, create more convincing lures, analyze more code, or identify more opportunities, the attacker has already become more productive. 

The 2026 Sophos Active Adversary Report describes the effect as more speed, volume, and noise in the threat landscape, even while attackers continue to use many of the same tools and techniques. 

Attackers have found a way to scale their operations. Most defenders have not. 

Organizations cannot patch at attacker speed 

This is especially visible in vulnerability management. 

The advice to “patch faster” is correct, but it does not reflect the full operational challenge. A security team cannot simply install every update as soon as it becomes available. 

Organizations need to know which systems are affected. They need to understand business criticality, test changes, coordinate maintenance windows, manage legacy technology, and confirm that remediation has worked. In some environments, a rushed update can create a significant operational outage. 

AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery and shortening the path between disclosure and exploitation. This raises the pressure on security teams that are already managing complex environments with limited resources. 

Many organizations simply do not have enough people to patch every system as quickly as the current threat environment requires. 

That does not necessarily mean they have a bad security program. It means their available capacity has not grown at the same rate as the problem. 

The gap between attacker speed and defender capacity is getting wider.

The challenge goes beyond patching

Patching is only part of the issue. 

Analysis of 661 incidents in the 2026 Sophos Active Adversary Report found that 67% of intrusions began with compromised credentials or other identity-related tactics. Attackers reached Active Directory in an average of three hours and 24 minutes. 

That leaves very little room for delay. 

Organizations need to patch vulnerable systems, strengthen identity controls, retain the right telemetry, monitor suspicious behavior, and provide coverage outside normal business hours. They also need a tested plan for what happens when those controls fail. 

At some point, almost every organization will need help answering four basic questions: 

  • What happened?
  • How far did the attacker get?
  • What do we need to contain?
  • What do we need to do next?

Those questions require experienced Incident Response professionals. 

Technology helps, but experience still matters 

AI and automation will make Incident Response teams more productive. 

They can help responders collect evidence, correlate information, summarize activity, identify patterns, and focus their attention on the areas that matter most. We should embrace those capabilities. 

But a serious security incident is not simply a technical investigation. 

It requires judgment. Responders must make decisions with incomplete information while coordinating with security, IT, legal teams, insurers, executives, and sometimes regulators or law enforcement. 

They also need to communicate clearly under pressure. They must separate what is known from what is suspected, explain the business risk, and help leaders make decisions that may have significant operational consequences. 

Technology can support that work. It does not eliminate the need for experienced people. 

Those people take time to develop.

Twenty percent may not be enough 

No one can forecast the exact number of Incident Response professionals the industry will need. 

But workforce plans should account for the signals we can already see. 

Security providers are hiring. Partners are expanding their teams. DFIR firms are looking for overflow capacity. Organizations are facing shorter attack timelines while struggling to patch and protect increasingly complex environments. 

At the same time, AI is helping threat actors do more with the resources they already have. 

Taken together, I believe these indicators point to Incident Response demand growing faster than the commonly cited 20% range. 

The industry needs to prepare for that now. 

We need to develop new analysts, create stronger career paths, retain experienced responders, and build better partnerships between internal security teams and external providers. We also need to use AI and automation to amplify the expertise we have, rather than assuming technology will remove the need for it.

Attackers are increasing their capacity.
Defenders must do the same. 

Sources

  • U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, “Information Security Analysts,” Occupational Outlook Handbook (2025–2035 outlook). View source
  • Sophos, “Sophos AI Security 2026 Report.” View source
  • Sophos, “Nowhere, man: The 2026 Active Adversary Report.” View source
  • Sophos, “Stopping real-world attacks: Lessons for business leaders from the 2026 cyber frontline.” View source
